request.instructions: You are a single agent working alone. Solve the task directly and completely. State your final answer explicitly on the last line, prefixed with 'Answer:'.

messages.content: Produce a rigorous technical brief on optimizing compiler internals. For EACH of the following areas you must discuss at least three specific named mechanisms in real depth: (1) SSA construction, (2) alias analysis, (3) register allocation, (4) inlining, (5) escape analysis, (6) loop vectorization, (7) instruction scheduling, (8) loop optimizations . Use precise standard terminology for every mechanism you name. Be exhaustive: a shallow mention of an area does not count as covering it.

response.content:
# Technical Brief: Optimizing Compiler Internals

## 1. SSA Construction

**Cytron et al. dominance-frontier algorithm.** The canonical approach builds SSA form in two phases. First, compute the dominator tree (typically via the Lengauer-Tarjan algorithm, O(E·log V), or the simpler iterative dataflow approach for smaller CFGs). Second, compute dominance frontiers: DF(n) is the set of nodes where n's dominance ends on some path. For each variable v, φ-functions are inserted at every node in the iterated dominance frontier of the set of blocks that define v. This is precise—it inserts the minimal number of φ-nodes needed for correctness (minimal/pruned SSA when combined with liveness filtering)—but requires global dataflow information (dominator tree + DF sets) before any renaming occurs. After insertion, a renaming pass walks the dominator tree depth-first, maintaining a stack of reaching definitions per variable, assigning fresh SSA names at each definition and φ-argument slot.

**Braun et al. "Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form" (local value numbering with incomplete φs).** This is the dominant approach in modern JIT and AOT compilers (e.g., used in LLVM's fast-isel paths and many sea-of-nodes JITs) because it builds SSA directly during a single forward pass over the CFG without precomputing dominance frontiers. Each basic block maintains a local map from variable to current SSA value. When a block is sealed (all predecessors known) and a variable lookup misses locally, the algorithm recursively queries predecessors. If a block has multiple predecessors, it optimistically inserts an "incomplete" φ-node, recurses into predecessors to fill operands, then runs φ-simplification: if all operands of a φ are identical (or the φ refers to itself), the φ is redundant and is replaced by that single value, with uses rewritten transitively. This handles loops via "unsealed" blocks—φs for loop headers are marked incomplete until the back edge's predecessor is processed, then recursively completed. The result is minimal SSA without a separate dominance computation, at the cost of needing a cleanup/simplification pass that is essentially a mini version of global value numbering.

**Sreedhar-Gao / linear-time dominance frontier via DJ-graphs.** For compilers needing to scale SSA construction to very large functions, direct dominance-frontier computation can be a bottleneck. Sreedhar and Gao's approach avoids materializing DF sets explicitly by augmenting the dominator tree with "join edges" (edges from the original CFG not captured by dominance, forming a DJ-graph), then propagating φ-insertion requirements upward through dominator-tree ancestors using the DJ-graph's join edges directly, achieving near-linear time without the O(N²) worst case that naive DF-set computation can hit on CFGs with many join points (e.g., deeply nested switch/case or exception-handling code).

**Memory/SSA and the treatment of non-scalar state.** All three mechanisms above are typically extended with Memory SSA (or "Heap SSA") to version memory effects: each store creates a new memory SSA value, and loads are connected to the nearest dominating store via use-def chains, with memory φ-nodes merging memory states at control-flow joins. This is essential because alias analysis and dead-store elimination operate on these memory versions rather than on individual variables.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's inclusion-based (subset-constraint) analysis.** Models each pointer-valued variable as a set variable; assignments generate subset constraints (p ⊇ {a} for `p = &a`, p ⊇ q for `p = q`, and conditional/dereference constraints for `p = *q` and `*p = q`). Solving is iterative worklist propagation to a fixed point over a constraint graph, giving flow-insensitive, context-insensitive points-to sets. Complexity is roughly O(n³) in the number of variables in the naive formulation, improved to near-cubic with online cycle detection (collapsing strongly-connected components in the constraint graph, since SCCs imply equal points-to sets) and offline variable substitution (precomputing which variables must have identical points-to sets before the main solve, e.g., via Hardekopf and Lin's HVN/HRU techniques). Andersen's is the precision baseline most whole-program alias analyses are measured against.

**Steensgaard's unification-based analysis.** Instead of subset constraints, equality constraints are used: assignment `p = q` unifies the points-to sets of p and q (via union-find), so if p can point to X and q can point to Y, after unification both point to {X, Y} and this fact propagates destructively. This gives near-linear time (O(n·α(n)) with union-find) at a substantial precision cost relative to Andersen's, since unification loses directionality—information flows both ways through an assignment rather than one. Steensgaard's is favored in contexts where compile-time budget dominates (e.g., some whole-program link-time optimizers) where cubic Andersen's doesn't scale.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA).** Rather than tracking points-to sets, TBAA assumes two memory accesses may alias only if their static types are compatible under the source language's aliasing rules—most concretely, C/C++'s strict aliasing rule, where an lvalue of one type may not generally alias storage declared with an incompatible type (with `char*` as the universal exception). LLVM implements this via `!tbaa` metadata nodes forming a type hierarchy (struct-path TBAA tracks not just the base type but the field-access path, e.g., distinguishing `struct.Foo::field_a` from `struct.Foo::field_b`), attached to load/store instructions, with a cheap tree-ancestor check replacing an expensive points-to query. This is unsound in the presence of type-punning that violates strict aliasing, which is why `-fno-strict-aliasing` disables it.

**Flow-sensitive and context-sensitive refinements.** Both Andersen's and Steensgaard's are usually flow-insensitive (one points-to set per variable for the whole program) and context-insensitive (one summary per function across all call sites). Precision-critical compilers add: (a) flow sensitivity via sparse points-to analysis keyed on SSA values rather than program points, piggybacking on the SSA form itself so each SSA name has its own points-to set, cheaply handling strong updates; (b) context sensitivity via call-site cloning or the CFL-reachability/summary-based formulation (treating the problem as context-free-language reachability over a graph with "balanced parenthesis" call/return edge labels), as in points-to analyses derived from Reps-Horwitz-Sagiv's IFDS framework. Also standard: alias analysis granularity distinctions—must-alias, may-alias, and no-alias facts feed directly into whether a redundant load can be eliminated (needs must-alias) versus whether two stores can be reordered (needs no-alias).

## 3. Register Allocation

**Chaitin-Briggs graph-coloring allocation.** Build an interference graph where nodes are live ranges (or webs) and edges connect live ranges simultaneously live. Allocation reduces to k-coloring this graph (k = number of physical registers). The algorithm repeatedly simplifies: push onto a stack any node with degree < k (such a node is "trivially colorable" no matter what its neighbors get, by the Briggs optimistic-coloring insight—Chaitin's original version only pushed and never attempted doubtfully-colorable nodes, while Briggs's refinement optimistically pushes degree-≥k nodes too and only spills if coloring actually fails during the select phase). If no node has degree < k, pick a spill candidate by a cost heuristic (spill cost / degree, approximating "cheap to spill, frequently interfering") and simplify past it, marking it a potential spill. Once the graph is reduced to empty, pop the stack and assign colors (select phase), avoiding colors used by already-colored neighbors; nodes that fail to get a color become actual spills, triggering rewriting (inserting loads/stores) and a repeat of the whole build-simplify-select loop. Coalescing (merging move-related live ranges that don't interfere, to eliminate the move) is interleaved conservatively—Briggs conservative coalescing only merges nodes if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of significant degree, avoiding coalescing that would itself induce spills.

**Linear scan allocation (Poletto-Sarkar).** Computes live intervals (a conservative approximation of live ranges as contiguous ranges over a linear instruction numbering, rather than precise live sets) and sorts intervals by start point. Sweeping left to right, it maintains a pool of free physical registers and an active set of currently-live intervals; when an interval starts, it's assigned a free register (or the active interval with the furthest-away end point is evicted/spilled if none are free—the "spill the one that lives longest" heuristic minimizes total spilled range). This is far cheaper than graph coloring (near-linear vs. the superlinear cost of building and coloring an interference graph) and is the standard choice for JIT compilers under compile-time pressure (e.g., early JVM client compiler, early-tier JIT stages). Precision is lower because it approximates true liveness with intervals, overestimating interference at points where the real live ranges have holes.

**SSA-based / Hack-Goos-Kleine-Palsberg allocation via interval graphs.** Because SSA form (with values live across a dominator-tree subtree in a biased way) has interference graphs that are provably chordal (perfect graphs) for programs whose live ranges are SSA values, coloring can be done without heuristics—chordal graphs are colorable in linear time by simplicial elimination ordering (e.g., via maximal cardinality search), with no risk of getting stuck needing a heuristic spill decision during coloring itself. Spilling is instead decided as a separate pre-pass (choosing which values to spill so the remaining interference graph's max clique size, i.e., register pressure, fits within k), decoupling the NP-hard spill-choice problem from the now-polynomial coloring problem. This underlies "SSA elimination"-style allocators used in LLVM's greedy allocator lineage and in academic SSA-based allocators.

**Second-chance / greedy allocation with live-range splitting (LLVM's `RAGreedy`).** A hybrid: live ranges are assigned priority by spill weight (use density / size), and the allocator greedily assigns registers in priority order; when a conflict is unavoidable, rather than spilling the whole live range it attempts live-range splitting—breaking a range at loop boundaries or basic-block boundaries into smaller pieces, each independently allocatable, with the hope that only a cold sub-range needs to be spilled while the hot sub-range gets a register. This includes region splitting, local splitting, and "last chance recoloring" (evicting an already-assigned lower-priority range to make room), making it effectively graph-coloring-adjacent but driven by cost heuristics and interval representations rather than an explicit chromatic-number computation.

## 4. Inlining

**Cost-benefit/heuristic inlining with a size-growth budget.** The standard production approach (GCC's `-finline-functions`, LLVM's inline cost model) computes a synthetic cost for a candidate callee (roughly: a weighted sum of instruction counts, penalized for things like calls-within-calls or unrollable loops, discounted for simplifications become possible post-inlining such as arguments being constants enabling constant-folding of the body) and compares it against a threshold modulated by call-site "hotness" (block frequency from profile data, or static heuristics like whether the call is inside a loop). LLVM's `InlineCost` analysis walks the callee's IR symbolically, tracking which instructions would simplify given the actual argument values at this call site (constant propagation through the prospective inline), and only commits to inlining if the resulting cost is below threshold, with special-cased bonuses for single-call-site functions (effectively free to inline, since there's no code duplication) and for callees marked `always_inline`.

**Bottom-up / top-down inlining order and the SCC-based inliner.** Mutual recursion and deep call chains make the order of inlining decisions matter. The standard structure (e.g., LLVM's `InlinerPass` operating on the call graph's SCCs in post-order / bottom-up) processes callees before callers so that by the time a caller is considered for inlining its own callees, its body already reflects any beneficial inlining decisions made within it—preventing combinatorial blowup from inlining a function before it has itself been shrunk by inlining-driven simplification, and giving each SCC a chance to reach a local fixed point before ascending the call graph.

**Partial inlining.** When a callee has a cheap "fast path" and an expensive "slow path" (commonly, an early-return guard clause followed by substantial work), full inlining duplicates the entire body into every caller even though most callers only exercise the cheap path. Partial inlining splits the callee into the guarded fast-path region and an out-of-line residual function retaining the slow path, inlining only the fast-path region at the call site with a call to the residual for the rare case. This is implemented via outlining (the inverse of inlining): identifying a single-entry/single-exit region (often via a dominator/postdominator analysis to find the guard-clause CFG shape) and extracting it into a new function.

**Devirtualization-driven inlining (speculative/guarded inlining).** For virtual or indirect calls, inlining requires first resolving the target. Techniques include: class hierarchy analysis (CHA)—if whole-program visibility shows only one concrete override exists for a virtual method, the call can be devirtualized unconditionally; and speculative/guarded devirtualization—when profile data shows a call site is monomorphic or dominated by one receiver type at runtime (polymorphic inline caches in JITs record this), the compiler inserts a runtime type check (guard) with the inlined body of the likely target on the fast path and a fallback indirect call (or deoptimization, in tiered JITs like HotSpot's C2 or V8's TurboFan) on the slow path. This is central to JIT performance on object-oriented code where static CHA alone can't resolve most call sites.

## 5. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph / points-to-based escape analysis (Choi-Gupta-style, used in the JVM's C2/Graal).** Builds a connection graph over objects (allocation sites) and reference variables, with edges representing "points-to" and "deferred" (assignment-chain) relations, then propagates escape states through this graph using a fixed-point worklist. Each object node is classified into one of three states: NoEscape (object is provably confined to the current method/thread and never escapes even into callees' visible state—eligible for stack allocation or scalar replacement), ArgEscape (object escapes into a called method via an argument but not into the heap or another thread—can't be purely stack-local but can still skip synchronization elision concerns across certain boundaries), and GlobalEscape (object may be reachable by another thread or stored into a static/heap location visible beyond the method, must be heap-allocated normally). Edges are added for every store (`a.f = b` adds a field edge), every call (parameters passed to unanalyzed/opaque callees force at least ArgEscape, modulo interprocedural summaries), and every return.

**Scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA) as the escape-analysis payoff.** Once an object is proven NoEscape, the compiler doesn't merely stack-allocate it—when possible it goes further and replaces the object's fields with independent SSA scalar values, eliminating the allocation and all field loads/stores entirely (the object becomes a set of virtual registers). This requires the escape analysis to also prove the object isn't accessed through a pointer that could alias it unpredictably (no aliasing ambiguity on the field accesses), which is why SROA is typically gated on both escape analysis and a simple local alias check. This is the mechanism behind eliminating allocations for things like temporary tuple/record objects or boxed values in managed-language JITs.

**Allocation sinking and partial escape analysis (Graal's approach).** Rather than a strict binary "escapes or not" classification before any optimization, partial escape analysis (as introduced in Stadler, Würthinger, Mössenböck's work used in Graal) performs the analysis interleaved with control-flow-sensitive virtualization: an object is kept "virtual" (not materialized) along every control-flow path where it doesn't escape, and only materialized (an actual allocation emitted) on the specific paths where it does escape—e.g., an object allocated and usually consumed locally but occasionally passed to a logging call on a rare branch only needs real allocation on that rare branch, while the common path keeps it virtual (scalar-replaced) the whole time. This is strictly more precise than a method-global escape classification because escape is decided per-control-flow-path rather than per-allocation-site.

**Thread-local/synchronization elision as an escape-analysis consumer.** A second major consumer of escape results beyond allocation elimination: if an object is proven to never escape the current thread (NoEscape or thread-confined classification), any `synchronized` blocks or locks guarding access to that object are provably uncontended and can be elided entirely (lock elision/biased locking removal), since no other thread can ever observe or contend for that monitor. This is a correctness-sensitive optimization, so it requires the escape analysis to be sound with respect to thread visibility, not merely heap visibility.

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**SLP (Superword-Level Parallelism) vectorization.** Rather than vectorizing a loop's iterations, SLP (Larsen-Amarasinghe) finds parallelism within a single loop iteration (or straight-line code) by packing isomorphic, independent scalar operations into vector operations. It builds "packs" bottom-up from seed candidates (adjacent memory accesses, e.g., consecutive array stores) and grows packs by following the def-use chains of the seed operations, merging further scalar instructions into the pack if they are isomorphic in opcode and the resulting pack has no cross-pack dependencies that would force a cycle in scheduling. This is the mechanism that vectorizes code that manually unrolls short fixed-length computations (e.g., a 4-wide `struct{x,y,z,w}` arithmetic block) without needing a surrounding countable loop at all.

**Loop-level (strip-mining) vectorization with a legality/cost model (LLVM's LoopVectorize).** The classical approach: determine the loop is countable with a known (possibly runtime) trip count, strip-mine it into chunks of width W (the target vector width), and replace the per-iteration scalar operations with their vector equivalents. Legality requires: no loop-carried dependencies that cross iterations within a single vector lane group in a way that breaks SIMD semantics (checked via dependence analysis, see below), and either no aliasing between accessed arrays or a runtime alias check inserted as a guard (if pointers *might* alias, the vectorizer can emit a cheap runtime bounds-disjointness check and fall back to the scalar loop if it fails—"loop versioning for vectorization"). The cost model compares the estimated cost of the vector loop (instruction count weighted by target-specific vector-instruction throughput/latency tables) against the scalar loop and only commits if profitable, also choosing the vectorization factor (VF) and interleave/unroll factor jointly to hide latency and amortize the strip-mining remainder-loop overhead.

**Loop dependence analysis for vectorization legality (GCD test, Banerjee's inequalities, dependence distance vectors).** To determine whether two array accesses across different loop iterations conflict (a true dependence that forbids reordering/parallel execution), compilers compute dependence distance and direction vectors. The GCD (greatest common divisor) test is a cheap necessary (not sufficient) condition: for subscripts expressed as linear functions of loop induction variables, a dependence can only exist if the GCD of the coefficients divides the constant difference between the two subscript expressions; if it doesn't divide evenly, no integer solution exists and the accesses provably never alias across iterations. Banerjee's inequalities refine this with bounds-aware range tests (using the known iteration-space bounds to determine whether the real-valued system of subscript equations has a solution within the loop's actual bounds), giving a more precise (but costlier) legality test than the GCD test alone. These feed directly into whether vectorization can proceed without a runtime check, versus needing the aliasing fallback mentioned above.

**Handling reductions and induction variables as special vectorizable idioms.** Standard reduction patterns (`sum += a[i]`) are not naively vectorizable because each iteration depends on the previous iteration's partial sum (a loop-carried dependence). Vectorizers special-case reduction idiom recognition: the loop body is transformed to accumulate W independent partial sums in a vector register across strip-mined iterations, with a final horizontal reduction (e.g., `vhadd`/shuffle-and-add tree) after the loop to combine the W lanes into the scalar result. Induction variables are similarly special-cased: rather than vectorizing the increment as a dependent chain, the vectorizer directly computes `base + lane_index*step` per lane (a vectorized induction recognized and rewritten structurally, not by naive SIMD translation of the scalar increment).

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling over the data-dependence DAG.** The baseline algorithm builds a DAG per basic block (or extended region) where nodes are instructions and edges represent true (RAW), anti (WAR), and output (WAW) dependences along with latency weights, then computes each node's priority (classically, its distance to the DAG's "bottom"—the critical-path length from this node to the end of the schedule, i.e., height in the DAG) and greedily picks, at each cycle, the highest-priority ready instruction (one whose predecessors are already scheduled and whose latencies have elapsed) from a ready list, subject to resource constraints (functional unit availability per cycle, modeled via a reservation table). Variants differ mainly in direction (top-down vs. bottom-up list scheduling) and tie-breaking heuristics (e.g., preferring instructions on the critical path, or that free up the most successors).

**Trace scheduling / superblock scheduling for scheduling across branches.** Basic-block-local scheduling can't hide latency across short blocks. Trace scheduling (Fisher) selects a likely execution path (a trace) spanning multiple basic blocks using profile-based branch probabilities, schedules across the whole trace as if it were straight-line code, and inserts compensation code at trace entry/exit points where control flow actually diverges from the selected trace (since instructions may have been hoisted above a branch that, off-trace, shouldn't execute them, or hoisted past a point where off-trace control flow expects them not yet executed). Superblock scheduling is a restricted, more tractable variant: it first tail-duplicates code so that superblocks have a single entry but allow multiple exits (removing all side entrances into the middle of the region by cloning), which simplifies the compensation-code problem since there's no "join" to reconcile mid-region.

**Software pipelining (modulo scheduling).** For loops, rather than scheduling one iteration's instructions, modulo scheduling overlaps multiple consecutive iterations' instructions so that a new iteration starts every II (initiation interval) cycles, where II is bounded below by both resource constraints (MinII from the busiest functional unit's usage per iteration) and recurrence constraints (RecMII from the longest latency cycle among loop-carried dependences, e.g., a loop-carried accumulator chain). The algorithm searches for the smallest feasible II (starting from max(MinII, RecMII) and incrementing on failure) and constructs a schedule, usually via a modulo reservation table that tracks resource usage modulo II across overlapped iterations. The resulting steady-state loop body executes code from several logical iterations concurrently, requiring prologue/epilogue code to fill and drain the overlapped pipeline. This is standard in VLIW/DSP and some high-end statically-scheduled architectures where hardware out-of-order execution isn't available to extract this ILP dynamically.

**Register-pressure-sensitive scheduling and the scheduling/allocation phase-ordering problem.** A purely latency-driven list scheduler can hoist instructions early to hide latency, which extends live ranges and increases register pressure, potentially causing spills that negate the scheduling benefit. Production schedulers add a pressure-aware tie-break or secondary priority: among ready instructions with equal latency-based priority, prefer the one that doesn't increase the number of simultaneously-live values (e.g., prefer consuming an already-live value over producing a new one, all else equal), or run a pre-pass pressure-reduction scheduling heuristic before the latency-driven pass. This reflects the broader phase-ordering tension between scheduling (wants long live ranges hoisted apart to hide latency) and register allocation (wants short live ranges), which some compilers address by interleaving or iterating the two phases rather than strictly sequencing them.

## 8. Loop Optimizations

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM).** Identifies computations inside a loop whose operands are all loop-invariant (defined outside the loop, or themselves invariant computations already hoisted) and hoists them to the loop's preheader (a dedicated single-entry block inserted immediately before the loop header specifically to give hoisted code somewhere safe to live without disturbing the loop's own entry edges). Soundness requires the hoisted instruction to be safe to speculate unconditionally (no possible trap/exception that wouldn't have occurred on the original conditional execution path, unless the loop is known to execute at least once) and, for stores, requires proving the location is written on every loop iteration with no other intervening aliasing access (this interacts directly with alias analysis).

**Strength reduction and induction variable simplification/canonicalization.** Within a loop, derived induction variables (e.g., `j = i*4` where `i` increments by 1 each iteration) are rewritten to be computed by simple addition each iteration (`j += 4`) instead of recomputing a multiply from `i` every time—replacing an expensive operation with a cheaper one that's algebraically equivalent given the loop's structure. This is typically implemented via LLVM's `IndVarSimplify`/SCEV (scalar evolution) machinery: every value in the loop derived from induction variables is expressed symbolically as a closed-form "add recurrence" `{start, +, step}`, and strength reduction rewrites each such chain into a single canonical induction variable plus cheap per-iteration updates, eliminating redundant induction variables entirely (induction variable elimination) when multiple IVs are mutually derivable.

**Loop unrolling (full and partial) and unroll-and-jam.** Partial unrolling replicates the loop body U times per iteration of a shrunk-trip-count loop, amortizing per-iteration overhead (branch, induction-variable update) and exposing more instruction-level parallelism and scheduling freedom across the now-larger body, at the cost of code size and (if done before vectorization) potentially interacting with the vectorizer's own interleaving factor. Full unrolling (eliminating the loop entirely) applies when the trip count is a known small compile-time constant, replacing the loop with straight-line code and enabling further constant folding/CSE across what were separate iterations. Unroll-and-jam specifically targets nested loops: it unrolls the outer loop and then fuses ("jams") the resulting multiple copies of the inner loop back into a single inner loop body containing U interleaved copies of the original inner-loop statements—useful when the inner loop reuses data across outer-loop iterations, improving cache reuse and giving the scheduler more independent work per inner iteration without the code-size blowup of fully unrolling the inner loop too.

**Loop fusion, fission (distribution), interchange, and tiling (blocking) as a dependence-driven family.** Loop fusion merges two adjacent loops with the same iteration space into one, reducing loop overhead and improving data locality (if both loops touch the same array, fusion can turn two cache-unfriendly passes into one), but is only legal if no dependence from the second loop targets an iteration of the first loop that hasn't executed yet (checked via dependence-direction analysis, same family of tests as vectorization legality). Loop fission is the inverse—splitting one loop into multiple loops over the same iteration space—done when a single loop body is too large for good register/cache behavior, or to isolate a vectorizable portion from a non-vectorizable one. Loop interchange swaps the nesting order of two loops (e.g., making the loop that strides contiguously through memory the innermost one) to improve spatial locality or to expose a vectorizable innermost loop, legal only when the dependence direction vectors permit reordering (specifically, no dependence has a direction vector that would require a "backward" direction in the interchanged order). Loop tiling (blocking) decomposes a loop's iteration space into smaller rectangular blocks sized to fit a target cache level, adding an extra level of loop nesting so that data reused across iterations stays resident in cache rather than being evicted and re-fetched—standard in optimizing dense linear algebra kernels, and often implemented through the polyhedral model (representing loop nests as integer points in a polytope defined by affine bounds, with transformations like tiling/interchange/fusion expressed as affine or piecewise-affine maps on that polytope, as in Graphite/Polly-style infrastructures), which generalizes these individual ad hoc transformations into a single unified affine-scheduling optimization problem.

---

Answer: See the full technical brief above, covering (1) SSA construction — Cytron et al. dominance-frontier algorithm, Braun et al. simple/incomplete-φ construction, Sreedhar-Gao DJ-graph linear-time DF computation, plus Memory SSA; (2) alias analysis — Andersen's inclusion-based analysis, Steensgaard's unification-based analysis, type-based alias analysis (TBAA), and flow-/context-sensitive refinements (sparse points-to, CFL-reachability/IFDS); (3) register allocation — Chaitin-Briggs graph coloring, linear scan (Poletto-Sarkar), SSA-based chordal-graph coloring (Hack-Goos et al.), and greedy allocation with live-range splitting (LLVM RAGreedy); (4) inlining — cost-benefit heuristic inlining with symbolic simplification, bottom-up SCC-ordered inlining, partial inlining via outlining, and CHA/speculative devirtualization-driven inlining; (5) escape analysis — connection-graph escape analysis (NoEscape/ArgEscape/GlobalEscape), scalar replacement of aggregates, partial escape analysis with allocation sinking (Graal), and synchronization/lock elision; (6) loop vectorization — SLP vectorization, strip-mining loop vectorization with legality/cost models, dependence analysis (GCD test, Banerjee's inequalities), and reduction/induction-variable idiom recognition; (7) instruction scheduling — list scheduling over dependence DAGs, trace/superblock scheduling, software pipelining (modulo scheduling), and register-pressure-sensitive scheduling; (8) loop optimizations — LICM, strength reduction/induction variable simplification via scalar evolution, loop unrolling and unroll-and-jam, and loop fusion/fission/interchange/tiling including the polyhedral model.
